questions.stem: Lack of sleep can ___ your memory.
questions.expl: After can, we need a base verb. Affect is the verb; effect is usually a noun.

questions.stem: The new rule had a positive ___ on sales.
questions.expl: After a positive, we need a noun. Effect is the noun meaning 'result'.

questions.stem: Could you ___ me some money until tomorrow?
questions.expl: Lend means 'give something for a short time': lend somebody something. Borrow means 'take', so it does not fit with me as the receiver.

questions.stem: I ___ a book from the library every week.
questions.expl: Borrow something from somewhere means you take it and give it back later.

questions.stem: Can you ___ me the way to the station?
questions.expl: Tell is followed by a person: tell me the way. Say and speak do not take a person as the object like this.

questions.stem: She ___ that she was tired.
questions.expl: Say that + clause. Told needs a person after it: told me that…

questions.stem: I always ___ my homework after dinner.
questions.expl: We say do homework. It is a fixed collocation.

questions.stem: Don't worry if you ___ a mistake.
questions.expl: We say make a mistake. It is a fixed collocation.

questions.stem: Could you ___ me a favor?
questions.expl: Do somebody a favour means 'help somebody'. It is a fixed expression.

questions.stem: We need to ___ a decision today.
questions.expl: We say make a decision. It is a fixed collocation.

questions.stem: Don't ___ your boarding pass.
questions.expl: After don't, we need a base verb: lose. Loose is an adjective; loss is a noun.

questions.stem: These pants are too ___ for me.
questions.expl: After too, we need an adjective. Loose means 'not tight'.

questions.stem: She has found a new ___ in a bank.
questions.expl: After a new, we need a singular countable noun. Job is countable; work in this sense is not.

questions.stem: I have a lot of ___ to do today.
questions.expl: A lot of + uncountable noun. Work is uncountable here, so it takes no a and no -s.

questions.stem: The party was really ___. We danced all night.
questions.expl: Fun means 'enjoyable'. Funny means 'making you laugh'.

questions.stem: He told a ___ joke and everyone laughed.
questions.expl: A joke that makes people laugh is funny.

questions.stem: I'm ___. There's nothing to do.
questions.expl: Bored describes how a person feels. Boring describes the thing that causes the feeling.

questions.stem: The lecture was so ___ that I fell asleep.
questions.expl: The lecture caused the feeling, so we use the -ing adjective: boring.

questions.stem: We were ___ by the amazing news.
questions.expl: We describes people's feelings, so we use the -ed adjective: excited.

questions.stem: I like to ___ to music while I study.
questions.expl: Listen to music means paying attention to it on purpose.

questions.stem: Did you ___ that noise?
questions.expl: Hear is for sounds that reach you without trying. A noise is something you hear.

questions.stem: Let's ___ a movie tonight.
questions.expl: We watch a movie: we look at something that moves for a period of time.

questions.stem: ___ at this photo! Isn't it cute?
questions.expl: Look at means 'turn your eyes towards'. Look! is often used to make someone notice something.

questions.stem: The company will ___ prices next month.
questions.expl: Raise takes an object (prices). Rise has no object.

questions.stem: The sun ___ in the east.
questions.expl: Rise has no object: the sun rises. Raise needs an object.

questions.stem: The house is ___ the bank and the school.
questions.expl: Between is used for two clear points: the bank and the school.

questions.stem: She is popular ___ her classmates.
questions.expl: Among is used for a group of people or things: her classmates.

questions.stem: I have lived here ___ 2018.
questions.expl: 2018 is a starting point, so we use since.

questions.stem: We have known each other ___ ten years.
questions.expl: Ten years is a length of time, so we use for.

questions.stem: Please turn off your phone ___ the meeting.
questions.expl: The meeting is a noun phrase, so we need the preposition during.

questions.stem: Someone called ___ you were out.
questions.expl: You were out is a clause, so we need the conjunction while.

questions.stem: ___ the heavy traffic, she arrived on time.
questions.expl: The heavy traffic is a noun phrase, so we need the preposition Despite.

questions.stem: ___ he was tired, he finished the report.
questions.expl: He was tired is a clause, so we need the conjunction Although.

questions.stem: The flight was delayed ___ the storm.
questions.expl: The storm is a noun phrase, so we need because of.

questions.stem: I stayed home ___ I was sick.
questions.expl: I was sick is a clause, so we need the conjunction because.

questions.stem: The country has seen strong ___ growth.
questions.expl: Economic means 'related to the economy': economic growth.

questions.stem: This small car is very ___ to run.
questions.expl: Economical means 'not costing much money or fuel'.

questions.stem: Can you give me some ___ about studying abroad?
questions.expl: Advice is an uncountable noun, so it has no -s. Advise is the verb.

questions.stem: The doctor ___ me to drink more water.
questions.expl: We need a past tense verb: advised. Advice is the noun.

questions.stem: Please ___ me to buy milk.
questions.expl: Remind somebody to do something means 'make somebody remember'.

questions.stem: I can't ___ her name.
questions.expl: Remember means to keep something in your own memory.

questions.stem: Please ___ your answers before you submit.
questions.expl: Check means 'look again to make sure it is correct'. Control means 'have power over'.

questions.stem: The lawyer has a meeting with a new ___ at ten.
questions.expl: A person who pays a lawyer or other professional is a client.

questions.stem: Hotel ___ can use the gym for free.
questions.expl: People staying at a hotel are guests.

questions.stem: Factory workers here are paid an hourly ___.
questions.expl: Money paid by the hour or week is a wage. A salary is paid monthly or yearly.

questions.stem: She won first ___ in the speech contest.
questions.expl: Something you win in a contest is a prize. Price is what something costs.

questions.stem: She has had a long and successful ___ as a doctor.
questions.expl: A career is the work a person does over many years.

questions.stem: We went on a business ___ to Singapore.
questions.expl: A short visit for work is a business trip.

questions.stem: The ___ from London to Edinburgh takes over four hours by train.
questions.expl: Journey means travel from one place to another, often a long one.

questions.stem: The dog is wagging ___ tail.
questions.expl: Its is the possessive: the tail belongs to the dog. It's means it is.

questions.stem: ___ raining. Take an umbrella.
questions.expl: It's = it is: It is raining.

questions.stem: This phone is cheaper ___ that one.
questions.expl: Comparatives use than: cheaper than.

questions.stem: I love fruit, ___ mangoes.
questions.expl: Especially means 'more than others; in particular'.

questions.stem: This cake was made ___ for your birthday.
questions.expl: Specially means 'for one particular purpose'.

questions.stem: She works very ___ to support her family.
questions.expl: Hard is also an adverb: work hard. Hardly means 'almost not'.

questions.stem: I could ___ hear him because of the noise.
questions.expl: Hardly means 'almost not': I could almost not hear him.

questions.stem: Have you seen any good movies ___?
questions.expl: Lately means 'recently' and is often used with the present perfect.

questions.stem: She likes to travel ___.
questions.expl: Alone means 'without other people'.

questions.stem: He felt ___ in the big city without friends.
questions.expl: Lonely describes the sad feeling of having no friends or company.

questions.stem: The final match was really ___.
questions.expl: The match caused the feeling, so we use the -ing adjective: exciting.

questions.stem: My brother ___ a doctor.
questions.expl: My brother = he, so the verb is is.

questions.stem: They ___ from a coastal city.
questions.expl: They goes with are.

questions.stem: I ___ not hungry right now.
questions.expl: I goes with am.

questions.stem: ___ your parents at home today?
questions.expl: Your parents is plural, so the question starts with Are.

questions.stem: The coffee ___ too hot.
questions.expl: Coffee is uncountable, so it takes a singular verb: is.

questions.stem: We ___ very excited about the trip.
questions.expl: We goes with are.

questions.stem: My keys ___ on the table.
questions.expl: My keys is plural, so the verb is are.

questions.stem: It ___ cold today. Wear a jacket.
questions.expl: It goes with is.

questions.stem: She [are] [a] good [teacher] [at] our school.
questions.expl: She is singular, so use is, not are.

questions.stem: My friends [is] [very] friendly [to] [everyone].
questions.expl: My friends is plural, so use are, not is.

questions.stem: I [tired] [today] because I [didn't] [sleep].
questions.expl: An adjective cannot follow the subject directly. English needs the verb to be: I am tired.

questions.stem: Are you ready for the test?
questions.expl: Present-simple be question: put Are before you, followed by the adjective ready.

questions.stem: My sister is a nurse.
questions.expl: Sister is singular, so use is. A singular countable job noun needs the article a.

questions.stem: They are not at school today.
questions.expl: They is plural, so use are. The negative form is are not, or aren't.

questions.stem: She ___ to work by bus every day.
questions.expl: She + present simple verb + -es: goes. Every day signals a habit.

questions.stem: My parents ___ TV in the evening.
questions.expl: My parents is plural, so the verb has no -s: watch.

questions.stem: Water ___ at 100 degrees Celsius.
questions.expl: This is a fact, and water is singular, so the verb takes -s: boils.

questions.stem: He ___ eat meat. He's a vegetarian.
questions.expl: He + doesn't + base verb.

questions.stem: ___ your sister speak English?
questions.expl: Your sister = she, so the question uses Does.

questions.stem: The train ___ at 7:30 every morning.
questions.expl: A fixed timetable uses the present simple. The train is singular: leaves.

questions.stem: I usually ___ up at six.
questions.expl: I + base verb. Usually signals the present simple.

questions.stem: Tom ___ his homework after dinner.
questions.expl: Tom = he, so do becomes does.

questions.stem: Cats ___ milk.
questions.expl: Cats is plural, so the verb has no -s: like.

questions.stem: She ___ never late for class.
questions.expl: She goes with is. Never comes after the verb to be.

questions.stem: My father [work] [in] a hospital [near] [our] house.
questions.expl: My father = he, so the verb needs -s: works.

questions.stem: She [doesn't] [likes] spicy [food] [at all].
questions.expl: After doesn't, use the base verb: like.

questions.stem: [Do] your brother [play] [the] guitar [well]?
questions.expl: Your brother = he, so the question starts with Does.

questions.stem: Alex always walks to school.
opts: Alex goes to school on foot every day.
Alex never goes to school on foot.
questions.expl: Always walks to school means the same as goes on foot every day.

questions.stem: She usually drinks tea in the morning.
questions.expl: With she in the present simple, the verb takes third-person -s: drinks.

questions.stem: Does your brother live in London?
questions.expl: Does starts a present-simple question, so the main verb stays in the base form live.

questions.stem: We don't go to school on Sundays.
questions.expl: We is plural, so use do not, or don't, before the base verb go.

questions.stem: I'll be back in ___ hour.
questions.expl: The h in hour is silent, so it starts with a vowel sound: an hour.

questions.stem: He studies at ___ university in the capital city.
questions.expl: University starts with a /j/ sound, which is a consonant sound: a university.

questions.stem: Look at ___ moon! It's so bright.
questions.expl: There is only one moon, so we use the.

questions.stem: My mother is ___ teacher.
questions.expl: A job after be needs a or an. Teacher starts with a consonant sound: a.

questions.stem: Can you close ___ door, please?
questions.expl: Both speakers know which door, so we use the.

questions.stem: She bought ___ umbrella yesterday.
questions.expl: Umbrella starts with a vowel sound, so we use an.

questions.stem: I love ___ music.
questions.expl: Music in general is uncountable, so no article is needed.

questions.stem: It's ___ European company.
questions.expl: European starts with a /j/ sound, which is a consonant sound: a European company.

questions.stem: She is [a] [honest] [and] kind [person].
questions.expl: The h in honest is silent, so we need an: an honest person.

questions.stem: I want [to] [be] [doctor] [when] I grow up.
questions.expl: A singular job needs an article: a doctor.

questions.stem: [The] life [is] [too] [short] to worry.
questions.expl: Life in general takes no article: Life is too short.

questions.stem: I have an idea.
questions.expl: Idea begins with a vowel sound, so use an before the singular noun.

questions.stem: The book on the table is mine.
questions.expl: The phrase on the table describes which book. Mine is a possessive pronoun, so it can stand alone after is.

questions.stem: There are five ___ in my family.
questions.expl: The usual plural of person is people.

questions.stem: Brush your ___ before bed.
questions.expl: Tooth has an irregular plural: teeth.

questions.stem: I bought two ___ of milk.
questions.expl: Box ends in -x, so it adds -es: boxes.

questions.stem: Tokyo and London are big ___.
questions.expl: A consonant + y changes to -ies: city → cities.

questions.stem: The ___ are playing in the garden.
questions.expl: Child has an irregular plural: children.

questions.stem: Can you give me some ___?
questions.expl: Advice is uncountable, so it has no -s.

questions.stem: There are three ___ in the box.
questions.expl: Mouse has an irregular plural: mice.

questions.stem: I have [two] [childs] and [a] [dog].
questions.expl: Child has an irregular plural: children.

questions.stem: She gave me [many] [useful] [informations] [about] the job.
questions.expl: Information is uncountable, so it has no -s.

questions.stem: There are many tourists in the city.
questions.expl: Tourists is plural, so use there are. Many is followed by a plural countable noun.

questions.stem: The shop opens ___ 8 o'clock.
questions.expl: A clock time takes at.

questions.stem: My birthday is ___ June 12th.
questions.expl: A date takes on.

questions.stem: We often go to the beach ___ summer.
questions.expl: A season takes in.

questions.stem: I'll call you ___ Friday.
questions.expl: A day of the week takes on.

questions.stem: She was born ___ 1999.
questions.expl: A year takes in.

questions.stem: There's a cat ___ the roof.
questions.expl: On a surface: on the roof.

questions.stem: I'll wait for you ___ the bus stop.
questions.expl: A specific point takes at: at the bus stop.

questions.stem: I usually study ___ night.
questions.expl: At night is a fixed expression.

questions.stem: He lives ___ Paris.
questions.expl: A city or town takes in.

questions.stem: We have a meeting ___ the afternoon.
questions.expl: A part of the day takes in: in the afternoon.

questions.stem: The concert [starts] [in] Saturday [at] [8 p.m.]
questions.expl: A day of the week takes on: on Saturday.

questions.stem: I [usually] [drink] coffee [at] the [morning].
questions.expl: A part of the day takes in: in the morning.

questions.stem: She [has] lived [at] Tokyo [since] [2020].
questions.expl: A city takes in: in Tokyo.

questions.stem: The class starts at seven in the morning.
questions.expl: Class is singular, so the present-simple verb takes -s: starts. Use at with a precise clock time.

questions.stem: We met on a rainy day in October.
questions.expl: Use the past simple met for a finished event. Use on with a particular day and in with a month.

questions.stem: There ___ a lot of people at the party.
questions.expl: People is plural, and the party is in the past, so we use were.

questions.stem: There ___ some water in the bottle.
questions.expl: Water is uncountable, so we use is.

questions.stem: ___ there any eggs in the fridge?
questions.expl: Eggs is plural, so the question is Are there.

questions.stem: There ___ two banks on this street.
questions.expl: Two banks is plural, so we use are.

questions.stem: There ___ a pen and two notebooks on my desk.
questions.expl: In a list, the verb agrees with the first noun: a pen, so is.

questions.stem: There isn't ___ sugar left.
questions.expl: Negative sentences usually use any.

questions.stem: [It] [has] a [beautiful] park [near] my house.
questions.expl: To say that something exists in a place, use There is, not It has.

questions.stem: There [is] [many] [interesting] [places] in the old city.
questions.expl: Places is plural, so we need There are.

questions.stem: There is a cat under the table.
questions.expl: Cat is singular, so use there is. Under tells us the cat's position relative to the table.

questions.stem: Are there any good restaurants near here?
questions.expl: Restaurants is plural, so the question begins Are there. Any is common in questions about an unspecified amount.

questions.stem: My little brother can ___ very fast.
questions.expl: Can + base verb: run.

questions.stem: When I was five, I ___ swim.
questions.expl: Ability in the past uses could.

questions.stem: ___ you help me with my homework, please?
questions.expl: Could you…? is a polite request.

questions.stem: Sorry, I ___ come to your party. I'm busy.
questions.expl: The negative of can is can't, followed by a base verb.

questions.stem: It's too dark. I ___ see anything.
questions.expl: Can't means 'not able to': I can't see anything.

questions.stem: She [can] [speaks] English [very] [well].
questions.expl: After can, use the base verb: speak.

questions.stem: I [can] [to] play [the] [piano].
questions.expl: Can is followed directly by the base verb. Delete to.

questions.stem: Can you play the guitar?
questions.expl: Can is a modal verb, so it is followed by the base verb play. The phrase play the guitar names the instrument.

questions.stem: Could you speak more slowly, please?
questions.expl: Could makes a polite request and is followed by the base verb speak. More slowly uses the adverb slowly to describe speaking.

questions.stem: She has ___.
questions.expl: Article + adjective + noun: a beautiful voice.

questions.stem: I ___ breakfast at home.
questions.expl: Frequency adverbs go before the main verb: usually have.

questions.stem: He is ___ late for work.
questions.expl: With the verb to be, the adverb comes after it: He is never late.

questions.stem: We [visited] [a] [museum famous] [in Paris] last year.
questions.expl: The adjective comes before the noun: a famous museum.

questions.stem: I [go] [often] [to the gym] [after work].
questions.expl: Frequency adverbs go before the main verb: I often go.

questions.stem: I met my best friend at school ten years ago.
questions.expl: Use the past simple met for a finished event. At school gives the place, and ten years ago gives a finished time in the past.

questions.stem: She always wears a black hat.
questions.expl: With she in the present simple, wear becomes wears. Always usually comes before the main verb.

questions.stem: We are going to visit our grandparents next week.
questions.expl: Be going to plus the base verb visit expresses a future plan. The time phrase next week places it in the future.

questions.stem: He bought an expensive watch for his father.
questions.expl: Bought is the past form of buy for a completed event. Expensive starts with a vowel sound, so use an before watch.

questions.stem: We ___ a great movie last night.
questions.expl: Last night is a finished past time, so we use the past simple.

questions.stem: She ___ to Japan two years ago.
questions.expl: Two years ago signals the past simple: go → went.

questions.stem: I ___ my keys yesterday, but I found them later.
questions.expl: The action finished in the past: lose → lost.

questions.stem: ___ you finish the report on time?
questions.expl: Past simple questions with ordinary verbs use Did.

questions.stem: They ___ at home last weekend.
questions.expl: They + past of be = were.

questions.stem: He didn't ___ the email.
questions.expl: Didn't + base verb: read.

questions.stem: When I was a child, I ___ in the countryside.
questions.expl: When I was a child is a finished past time, so we use the past simple.

questions.stem: The company ___ a new product in March.
questions.expl: In March (already past) signals the past simple.

questions.stem: I ___ very tired after the trip.
questions.expl: I + past of be = was.

questions.stem: She ___ her phone at home this morning.
questions.expl: Leave has an irregular past: left.

questions.stem: I [didn't] [went] to [the] party [last night].
questions.expl: After didn't, use the base verb: go.

questions.stem: We [buyed] [a] new car [two months] [ago].
questions.expl: Buy has an irregular past: bought.

questions.stem: [Did] she [called] you [yesterday] [evening]?
questions.expl: After Did, use the base verb: call.

questions.stem: I started learning English five years ago.
opts: I haven't learned English for five years.
I have learned English for five years.
I will learn English in five years.
questions.expl: Started five years ago and still learning = have learned for five years.

questions.stem: We went to the beach last Sunday.
questions.expl: Use the past simple went for a completed trip. Last Sunday is a finished time expression, so no present-perfect form is needed.

questions.stem: Did you enjoy the concert?
questions.expl: Did already marks the past tense, so the main verb returns to the base form enjoy.

questions.stem: She didn't have breakfast this morning.
questions.expl: Didn't is did not, so it carries the past tense and must be followed by the base form have.

questions.stem: Be quiet! The baby ___.
questions.expl: The action is happening now: is sleeping.

questions.stem: Look! Those people ___ the bus.
questions.expl: Look! shows it is happening now. Those people is plural: are getting off.

questions.stem: I ___ the answer to this question.
questions.expl: Know is a state verb, so it is not used in the continuous.

questions.stem: She ___ for her exam at the moment.
questions.expl: At the moment signals the present continuous.

questions.stem: We ___ dinner with my parents tonight. We booked a table.
questions.expl: An arranged plan for the near future uses the present continuous.

questions.stem: Prices ___ higher and higher these days.
questions.expl: A changing trend uses the present continuous: are getting.

questions.stem: Listen! Someone ___ at the door.
questions.expl: Listen! shows it is happening now.

questions.stem: Right now she [is] [cook] dinner [for] [her family].
questions.expl: Be + -ing: is cooking.

questions.stem: I [am] [wanting] [a] cup of [coffee].
questions.expl: Want is a state verb, so it is not used in the continuous: I want.

questions.stem: Look! The children [plays] [in] [the] [garden].
questions.expl: Look! shows the action is happening now: are playing.

questions.stem: What are you doing right now?
questions.expl: The question asks about an action happening now, so use present continuous: are plus doing.

questions.stem: My sister is working from home this week.
questions.expl: Present continuous can describe a temporary situation around now. With my sister, use is working.

questions.stem: This hotel is ___ than the one we stayed in last year.
questions.expl: Long adjectives form the comparative with more: more comfortable.

questions.stem: Today is ___ day of the year.
questions.expl: Short adjectives form the superlative with the + -est. Hot doubles the t: the hottest.

questions.stem: My English is getting ___.
questions.expl: Good has an irregular comparative: better.

questions.stem: This is ___ restaurant in town.
questions.expl: Long adjectives form the superlative with the most: the most expensive.

questions.stem: Her new car is ___ as mine.
questions.expl: Equal comparison uses as + adjective + as.

questions.stem: The weather today is ___ than yesterday.
questions.expl: Bad has an irregular comparative: worse.

questions.stem: Sam is ___ than her sister.
questions.expl: Short adjective + -er + than: taller than.

questions.stem: Of all the candidates, Mr. Kim is ___ qualified.
questions.expl: Of all the candidates shows a superlative: the most qualified.

questions.stem: This book [is] [more] [interesting] [then] the film.
questions.expl: Comparatives use than, not then. Then means 'after that'.

questions.stem: He [is] [more] [taller] [than] his brother.
questions.expl: Taller is already comparative. Delete more.

questions.stem: This is [the] [most] [cheap] [phone] in the shop.
questions.expl: Cheap is a short adjective, so the superlative is the cheapest.

questions.stem: Mount Everest is the highest mountain in the world.
questions.expl: Use the superlative highest to compare Everest with every other mountain in the world. The superlative normally takes the.

questions.stem: My room is bigger than yours.
questions.expl: Use the comparative adjective bigger for a comparison between two rooms, followed by than and the comparison yours.

questions.stem: How ___ people came to the meeting?
questions.expl: People is countable, so we use many.

questions.stem: We don't have ___ time. Let's hurry.
questions.expl: Time in this sense is uncountable, so we use much.

questions.stem: There are only ___ seats left. Book now!
questions.expl: Seats is countable, and the meaning is 'some, but not many': a few.

questions.stem: Could I have ___ water, please?
questions.expl: Polite requests and offers use some.

questions.stem: I didn't buy ___ bread.
questions.expl: Negative sentences usually use any.

questions.stem: She has ___ furniture in her new apartment.
questions.expl: Furniture is uncountable, so we use little, not few or many.

questions.stem: ___ of the information in this report is out of date.
questions.expl: Information is uncountable, so we use much.

questions.stem: ___ employees have asked to work from home.
questions.expl: Employees is a plural countable noun, so we use several.

questions.stem: How [many] [money] [do] you [need]?
questions.expl: Money is uncountable, so we say How much.

questions.stem: We [have] [a lot of] [homeworks] [today].
questions.expl: Homework is uncountable, so it has no -s.

questions.stem: There [isn't] [many] [milk] [left].
questions.expl: Milk is uncountable, so we use much.

questions.stem: There are a few apples in the basket.
questions.expl: Apples is countable and plural, so a few means a small positive number. Use are with there.

questions.stem: I need a little help with this.
questions.expl: Help is uncountable here, so use a little for a small positive amount. A little comes before the noun.

questions.stem: The phone is ringing. — OK, I ___ it.
questions.expl: A decision made at the moment of speaking uses will.

questions.stem: We've saved money because we ___ a new house next year.
questions.expl: A plan made before now uses be going to.

questions.stem: Watch out! That glass ___ fall!
questions.expl: A prediction based on what you can see now uses be going to.

questions.stem: I think the team ___ the match.
questions.expl: A prediction based on opinion (I think) uses will.

questions.stem: I promise I ___ tell anyone.
questions.expl: Promises use will. The negative is won't.

questions.stem: The new branch ___ next spring, according to the manager.
questions.expl: Next spring is in the future: will open.

questions.stem: I [will] [to] [call] you [tomorrow].
questions.expl: Will is followed by the base verb without to. Delete to.

questions.stem: She [going] [to] [start] a new job [next week].
questions.expl: Going to needs the verb to be: She is going to.

questions.stem: I'm going to learn ten new words every day.
questions.expl: Be going to plus learn expresses an intention or plan. Ten new words is the object, and every day gives the routine time.

questions.stem: Don't worry, I will help you.
questions.expl: Will plus the base verb help expresses a future decision or promise. The base form follows will.

questions.stem: You look tired. You ___ go to bed early.
questions.expl: Advice uses should.

questions.stem: Students ___ use phones during the exam. It's not allowed.
questions.expl: Something that is not allowed uses mustn't.

questions.stem: Tomorrow is Sunday, so I ___ get up early.
questions.expl: Something that is not necessary uses don't have to.

questions.stem: All visitors ___ sign in at reception.
questions.expl: A rule or obligation uses must.

questions.stem: He ___ wear a uniform at work.
questions.expl: With he, have to becomes has to.

questions.stem: You [must] [to] [finish] this [by Friday].
questions.expl: Must is followed by the base verb without to. Delete to.

questions.stem: My mother [have] [to] work [on] [weekends].
questions.expl: My mother = she, so have to becomes has to.

questions.stem: It isn't necessary to bring food.
opts: You don't have to bring food.
questions.expl: Not necessary = don't have to. Mustn't means it is not allowed.

questions.stem: You should practice speaking every day.
questions.expl: Should is a modal verb, so it is followed by the base form practice. Every day gives the recommended routine.

questions.stem: This isn't my umbrella. It's ___.
questions.expl: With no noun after it, we need the possessive pronoun hers (= her umbrella).

questions.stem: Please give ___ the report by noon.
questions.expl: After the verb give, we need an object pronoun: me.

questions.stem: Ms. Brown asked ___ assistant to book a room.
questions.expl: Before the noun assistant, we need a possessive adjective: her.

questions.stem: The children cleaned the room by ___.
questions.expl: By + reflexive pronoun means 'without help': by themselves.

questions.stem: Our team finished ___ project early.
questions.expl: Team is singular here, so the possessive is its. It's means it is.

questions.stem: Mr. Lee will present the results ___ because his assistant is sick.
questions.expl: Himself emphasises that he does it, not someone else.

questions.stem: [Me] and my brother [went] [to the zoo] [yesterday].
questions.expl: The subject needs a subject pronoun, and I usually comes last: My brother and I.

questions.stem: Is [this] pen [yours] or [hers]? — It's [my].
questions.expl: With no noun after it, we need the possessive pronoun mine.

questions.stem: The company [announced] [it's] new [policy] [yesterday].
questions.expl: The possessive is its. It's means it is.

questions.stem: Their house is bigger than ours.
questions.expl: Their shows possession before house. Ours is a possessive pronoun that replaces our house after the comparison.

questions.stem: I taught myself to play the guitar.
questions.expl: Taught myself uses a reflexive pronoun because the subject and the person receiving the action are the same.

questions.stem: I ___ this movie three times.
questions.expl: An experience up to now (three times) uses the present perfect.

questions.stem: She ___ in this company since 2018.
questions.expl: Since 2018 shows a situation that continues to now: present perfect.

questions.stem: Have you finished your report ___?
questions.expl: Questions in the present perfect often end with yet.

questions.stem: We ___ to a coastal city last summer.
questions.expl: Last summer is a finished past time, so we use the past simple.

questions.stem: He has ___ left the office. You just missed him.
questions.expl: Just means 'a very short time ago' and goes with the present perfect.

questions.stem: ___ you ever eaten durian?
questions.expl: Ever asks about experience: Have you ever…?

questions.stem: Sales ___ by 15 percent so far this year.
questions.expl: So far shows a period up to now: present perfect.

questions.stem: I haven't seen her ___ we graduated.
questions.expl: Since + a starting point, which can be a past clause.

questions.stem: They have been married ___ ten years.
questions.expl: For + a length of time: for ten years.

questions.stem: Ms. Garcia ___ as our marketing director for the past five years.
questions.expl: For the past five years continues up to now: present perfect.

questions.stem: I [have] [visited] my grandparents [last] [weekend].
questions.expl: Last weekend is a finished past time, so use the past simple: I visited.

questions.stem: She [has] [went] to [the] [bank].
questions.expl: Has + past participle: go → gone.

questions.stem: We [have] lived [here] [since] [five years].
questions.expl: Five years is a length of time, so use for, not since.

questions.stem: I started working here in 2020.
questions.expl: Started in 2020 and still working = have worked here since 2020.

questions.stem: This is the first time I have eaten sushi.
opts: I have never eaten sushi before.
questions.expl: The first time I have eaten it = I have never eaten it before.

questions.stem: Have you ever been to Japan?
questions.expl: Present perfect have been asks about experience up to now. Ever is common in questions about whether something has happened at any time.

questions.stem: I have just finished my homework.
questions.expl: Present perfect have finished connects a completed action with now. Just means the action happened very recently.

questions.stem: The new library ___ next year.
questions.expl: The library is opened by someone, in the future: will be opened.

questions.stem: These cars ___ in Japan.
questions.expl: The cars are made by someone: present simple passive.

questions.stem: The winners ___ at the end of the ceremony.
questions.expl: The winners are announced by someone, in the future: will be announced.

questions.stem: All applications must ___ by May 31.
questions.expl: Applications are submitted by people: must be + past participle.

questions.stem: The package ___ yesterday afternoon.
questions.expl: Yesterday + passive: was delivered.

questions.stem: The room ___ every morning by the hotel staff.
questions.expl: The room is cleaned by the staff every morning: present simple passive.

questions.stem: The meeting has ___ until next Thursday.
questions.expl: Present perfect passive: has been + past participle.

questions.stem: Customers ___ to keep their receipts.
questions.expl: Customers receive the advice: are advised.

questions.stem: The museum ___ by thousands of tourists every year.
questions.expl: The museum is visited by tourists: present simple passive.

questions.stem: This song [was] [wrote] [by] a [famous] singer.
questions.expl: The passive uses the past participle: written.

questions.stem: The documents [must] [send] [to] the [manager] today.
questions.expl: Documents are sent by someone: must be sent.

questions.stem: The house [is] [painting] [by] my father [right now].
questions.expl: Continuous passive: is being painted.

questions.stem: Someone stole my bike last night.
opts: My bike was stolen last night.
Someone's bike was stolen by me.
My bike has stolen last night.
questions.expl: The bike receives the action: My bike was stolen.

questions.stem: The office is cleaned every evening.
questions.expl: This is present simple passive: the office receives the action, so use is plus the past participle cleaned.

questions.stem: The results will be announced tomorrow.
questions.expl: This is future passive: the results receive the action, so use will be plus the past participle announced.

questions.stem: If you ___ hard, you will pass the exam.
questions.expl: First conditional: If + present simple.

questions.stem: If I ___ you, I would talk to her.
questions.expl: Second conditional: If I were you.

questions.stem: If I had more time, I ___ learn another language.
questions.expl: Second conditional: would + base verb.

questions.stem: If you mix red and white, you ___ pink.
questions.expl: A general fact uses the zero conditional: present simple in both parts.

questions.stem: ___ you hurry, you'll miss the bus.
questions.expl: Unless means 'if not': if you don't hurry, you'll miss the bus.

questions.stem: If the shipment ___ late, please contact our office.
questions.expl: First conditional: If + present simple.

questions.stem: We would hire more staff if our budget ___ larger.
questions.expl: Second conditional: if + were.

questions.stem: If she ___ the answer, she would tell us.
questions.expl: Second conditional: If + past simple.

questions.stem: If it [will] [rain] tomorrow, we [will] [stay] at home.
questions.expl: The if-clause in a first conditional does not use will: If it rains.

questions.stem: If I [have] [a car], I [would] [drive] to work.
questions.expl: Second conditional: If + past simple, so have becomes had.

questions.stem: [Unless] you [don't] [study], you [will] fail.
questions.expl: Unless already means 'if not'. Delete don't.

questions.stem: I don't have a car, so I can't drive you home.
opts: If I had a car, I could drive you home.
If I have a car, I can drive you home.
Unless I have a car, I could drive you home.
If I had a car, I can't drive you home.
questions.expl: An imagined present situation uses the second conditional.

questions.stem: If you need help, just call me.
questions.expl: In a first conditional, use present simple after if. The result here is an imperative: just call me.

questions.stem: What would you do if you won the lottery?
questions.expl: This is a second conditional for an imaginary situation. Use past simple won after if and would plus the base verb do in the result.

questions.stem: The girl ___ is sitting next to Tom is my cousin.
questions.expl: A person as the subject of the clause: who.

questions.stem: I lost the book ___ you lent me.
questions.expl: For a thing, we use which.

questions.stem: This is the restaurant ___ we had our first date.
questions.expl: For a place (= at which), we use where.

questions.stem: He's the student ___ father is a famous singer.
questions.expl: Whose shows possession: the student's father.

questions.stem: Applicants ___ have experience will be preferred.
questions.expl: People as the subject of the clause: who.

questions.stem: The laptop, ___ I bought last month, has already broken.
questions.expl: After a comma, use which for things, not that.

questions.stem: The company ___ products we use is based in Korea.
questions.expl: Whose shows possession: the company's products.

questions.stem: Employees ___ wish to attend the seminar should register by Friday.
questions.expl: People as the subject of the clause: who.

questions.stem: The man [which] [is] talking [to] my father [is] my teacher.
questions.expl: For a person, use who.

questions.stem: Paris, [that] [is] famous [for] art, [is] beautiful.
questions.expl: After a comma, use which, not that.

questions.stem: That is the house [which] my grandfather [built] [it] [in 1970].
questions.expl: Which already replaces the house. Delete it.

questions.stem: The book that I am reading is very interesting.
questions.expl: That introduces a relative clause describing the book. The present continuous am reading shows the action in progress now.

questions.stem: She is the teacher who helped me most.
questions.expl: Who introduces a relative clause about a person and acts as the subject of helped.

questions.stem: I really enjoy ___ to music.
questions.expl: Enjoy + -ing.

questions.stem: She decided ___ a new car.
questions.expl: Decide + to + verb.

questions.stem: We are looking forward to ___ you next week.
questions.expl: Look forward to + -ing. Here to is a preposition.

questions.stem: Would you mind ___ the window?
questions.expl: Mind + -ing.

questions.stem: He promised ___ me with my homework.
questions.expl: Promise + to + verb.

questions.stem: Thank you for ___ me.
questions.expl: After a preposition (for), use -ing.

questions.stem: Please remember ___ the lights when you leave.
questions.expl: Remember to do = don't forget to do something in the future.

questions.stem: The manager suggested ___ the meeting to Friday.
questions.expl: Suggest + -ing.

questions.stem: We cannot afford ___ any more delays.
questions.expl: Afford + to + verb.

questions.stem: Before ___ the office, please turn off your computer.
questions.expl: After a preposition (before), use -ing.

questions.stem: I [am] interested [in] [learn] [Japanese].
questions.expl: After a preposition (in), use -ing: learning.

questions.stem: She [avoided] [to answer] [my] [question].
questions.expl: Avoid + -ing: answering.

questions.stem: They [agreed] [helping] us [move] [house].
questions.expl: Agree + to + verb: to help.

questions.stem: I'm thinking about changing my job.
questions.expl: A preposition such as about is followed by a noun or gerund. Therefore use changing, not the infinitive change.

questions.stem: She wants to become a doctor.
questions.expl: Want is followed by to plus the base verb. Become is the base form after to.

questions.stem: ___ the high price, the tickets sold out quickly.
questions.expl: The high price is a noun phrase, so we need Despite.

questions.stem: ___ the store was busy, the staff were very patient.
questions.expl: The store was busy is a clause, so we need Although.

questions.stem: The event was postponed ___ the storm.
questions.expl: The storm is a noun phrase, so we need due to.

questions.stem: Please do not use your phone ___ the presentation.
questions.expl: The presentation is a noun phrase, so we need during.

questions.stem: Mr. Chen called ___ you were at lunch.
questions.expl: You were at lunch is a clause, so we need while.

questions.stem: She got the job ___ she had little experience.
questions.expl: She had little experience is a clause, so we need even though.

questions.stem: Sales increased ___ the successful advertising campaign.
questions.expl: The successful advertising campaign is a noun phrase, so we need because of.

questions.stem: The road is closed ___ repairs are being made.
questions.expl: Repairs are being made is a clause, so we need because.

questions.stem: [Despite] [it] was raining, [we] [played] football.
questions.expl: It was raining is a clause, so use Although, not Despite.

questions.stem: We [stayed] inside [because] [the heavy] [rain].
questions.expl: The heavy rain is a noun phrase, so use because of.

questions.stem: [During] I [was] [in Rome], I [visited] many museums.
questions.expl: I was in Rome is a clause, so use While, not During.

questions.stem: Although he was tired, he finished the work.
opts: Despite being tired, he finished the work.
Despite he was tired, he finished the work.
Because he was tired, he finished the work.
He was tired, so he didn't finish the work.
questions.expl: Although + clause = Despite + -ing: Despite being tired.

questions.stem: Despite the traffic, we arrived on time.
questions.expl: Despite is followed by a noun phrase, not a complete clause. The traffic is the noun phrase, and arrived is the main verb.

questions.stem: The price of these shoes ___ too high.
questions.expl: The real subject is the price (singular): is.

questions.stem: Each of the rooms ___ a private bathroom.
questions.expl: Each of + noun takes a singular verb: has.

questions.stem: The number of tourists ___ increased this year.
questions.expl: The number of takes a singular verb: has.

questions.stem: A number of customers ___ complained about the noise.
questions.expl: A number of + plural noun takes a plural verb: have.

questions.stem: Neither the manager nor the employees ___ aware of the change.
questions.expl: With neither…nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject (the employees): were.

questions.stem: Everyone in the office ___ the new coffee machine.
questions.expl: Everyone takes a singular verb: likes.

questions.stem: The information you gave me ___ very useful.
questions.expl: Information is uncountable, so the verb is singular: was.

questions.stem: The boxes [on] the shelf [is] [full] [of] books.
questions.expl: The real subject is the boxes (plural): are.

questions.stem: Every [one] of the students [have] [a] [book].
questions.expl: Every one of takes a singular verb: has.

questions.stem: The news [are] [very] [good] [today].
questions.expl: News is uncountable, so it takes a singular verb: is.

questions.stem: Each of the students has a different idea.
questions.expl: Each is grammatically singular even when it refers to several students, so use has.

questions.stem: The manager made an important ___ yesterday.
questions.expl: After the adjective important, we need a noun: decision.

questions.stem: Please drive ___ in the school zone.
questions.expl: The word describes the verb drive, so we need an adverb: carefully.

questions.stem: Our new product has been very ___.
questions.expl: After be (has been very), we need an adjective: successful.

questions.stem: She is a highly ___ engineer.
questions.expl: Before the noun engineer, we need an adjective: qualified.

questions.stem: The company has ___ expanded into Asia.
questions.expl: Between has and the past participle, we need an adverb: recently.

questions.stem: We appreciate your ___ in this matter.
questions.expl: After your, we need a noun: cooperation.

questions.stem: The instructions are not very ___.
questions.expl: After be, we need an adjective: clear.

questions.stem: Mr. Park will ___ the new staff members on Monday.
questions.expl: After will, we need a base verb: train.

questions.stem: Customer ___ is our top priority.
questions.expl: Customer satisfaction is a compound noun and the subject of the sentence.

questions.stem: The team worked ___ to meet the deadline.
questions.expl: Hard is also an adverb: work hard. Hardly means 'almost not'.

questions.stem: She [sings] [beautiful] [at] every [party].
questions.expl: The word describes the verb sings, so we need an adverb: beautifully.

questions.stem: This [is] a [very] [danger] [road].
questions.expl: Before the noun road, we need an adjective: dangerous.

questions.stem: She [thanked] us [for] [our] help and [patient].
questions.expl: And joins it to the noun help, so we need another noun: patience.

questions.stem: She answered all the questions correctly.
questions.expl: Correctly is an adverb modifying the verb answered. The past form answered matches the completed action.

questions.stem: When I got to the station, the train ___.
questions.expl: The train left before I arrived: past perfect.

questions.stem: By the time the manager arrived, we ___ the meeting.
questions.expl: By the time + past simple, then had + past participle.

questions.stem: She told me she ___ the movie before.
questions.expl: She saw the movie before the time she told me: had seen.

questions.stem: After he ___ his homework, he went out to play.
questions.expl: He finished his homework first, then went out: had finished.

questions.stem: I didn't recognize her because she ___ so much.
questions.expl: The change happened before I saw her: had changed.

questions.stem: The report ___ before the director requested it.
questions.expl: The report was finished before the request, and it received the action: had been completed.

questions.stem: When we [got] home, [someone] [has broken] [into] the house.
questions.expl: The break-in happened before we got home: had broken.

questions.stem: She [had] [went] to bed [before] I [called].
questions.expl: Had + past participle: go → gone.

questions.stem: I had never seen snow before I went to Japan.
questions.expl: Use past perfect had never seen for the earlier experience, followed by simple past went for the later event.

questions.stem: By the time we arrived, the party had ended.
questions.expl: By the time introduces a later past reference point, so the earlier event uses past perfect had ended.

questions.stem: If I ___ about the meeting, I would have attended.
questions.expl: Third conditional: If + had + past participle.

questions.stem: If we had left earlier, we ___ the flight.
questions.expl: Third conditional: would have + past participle.

questions.stem: If she had taken the job in Singapore, she ___ there now.
questions.expl: Mixed conditional: a past condition with a result now uses would + verb.

questions.stem: ___ the weather been better, the event would have been held outdoors.
questions.expl: Inverted third conditional: Had + subject + past participle.

questions.stem: You would have passed if you ___ harder.
questions.expl: Third conditional: if + had + past participle.

questions.stem: If I [would have] [known], I [would have] [called] you.
questions.expl: The if-clause does not take would. Third conditional: If I had known.

questions.stem: If he [had] [listened] to me, he [wouldn't] [make] that mistake.
questions.expl: A result in the past needs would have + past participle: wouldn't have made.

questions.stem: I didn't know her number, so I didn't call her.
opts: Unless I knew her number, I called her.
If I had known her number, I would have called her.
If I knew her number, I would call her.
If I had known her number, I would call her yesterday.
questions.expl: An imagined past situation uses the third conditional.

questions.stem: If I had saved more money, I would have bought that laptop.
questions.expl: This is a third conditional about an unreal past condition: past perfect after if and would have plus the past participle bought in the result.

questions.stem: She said that she ___ busy that day.
questions.expl: After said, the tense moves back: is → was.

questions.stem: He asked me where I ___.
questions.expl: Reported questions use statement word order, and the tense moves back: where I worked.

questions.stem: The doctor ___ me to get more rest.
questions.expl: Told + person + to + verb.

questions.stem: They asked ___ we could join them for dinner.
questions.expl: A reported yes/no question uses if or whether.

questions.stem: Sam said she ___ call me the next day.
questions.expl: After said, the tense moves back: will → would.

questions.stem: She [asked] me [where] [did I] [go] last weekend.
questions.expl: Reported questions use statement word order: where I had gone.

questions.stem: He [said] [me] [that] he [was] tired.
questions.expl: Say is not followed directly by a person. Use told me, or just said.

questions.stem: "I'm learning Japanese," said Alex.
opts: Alex said that she was learning Japanese.
Alex told that she learns Japanese.
Alex said she had learned Japanese.
Alex said that I am learning Japanese.
questions.expl: The tense moves back (am learning → was learning) and I becomes she.

questions.stem: She asked me if I liked spicy food.
questions.expl: In reported yes-or-no questions, use if and normal statement word order: I liked, not did I like.

questions.stem: The documents ___ by the lawyer are on your desk.
questions.expl: The documents were prepared by the lawyer (passive): prepared.

questions.stem: Employees ___ to attend the training should register online.
questions.expl: Employees who wish (active): wishing.

questions.stem: ___ the instructions, he assembled the desk easily.
questions.expl: He read the instructions first, then assembled the desk: Having read.

questions.stem: Any items ___ in the room will be kept at reception.
questions.expl: The items were left by someone (passive): left.

questions.stem: The man ___ to the manager is our new client.
questions.expl: The man who is talking (active): talking.

questions.stem: When ___ abroad, always carry a copy of your passport.
questions.expl: When + -ing, with you as the hidden subject: When travelling.

questions.stem: The [letter] [writing] by my grandfather [is] [very] old.
questions.expl: The letter was written by my grandfather (passive): written.

questions.stem: [Looking] out of the window, [the] [mountains] [were] beautiful.
questions.expl: The mountains cannot look out of the window. The two parts need the same subject, so use a full clause: When I looked.

questions.stem: The man standing at the door is my uncle.
questions.expl: Standing at the door is a reduced relative clause meaning who is standing at the door. The -ing form describes the man.

questions.stem: I wish I ___ how to swim.
questions.expl: A wish about the present uses the past simple: knew.

questions.stem: She wishes she ___ the bus this morning.
questions.expl: A wish about the past (this morning) uses had + past participle: hadn't missed.

questions.stem: If only I ___ taller!
questions.expl: If only + were for an unreal present.

questions.stem: I wish my neighbors ___ so much noise at night.
questions.expl: To wish that someone else would change, use would: wouldn't make.

questions.stem: I wish I [can] [speak] [Korean] [well].
questions.expl: A wish about the present moves can back to could.

questions.stem: He wishes he [didn't] [spend] [all his money] [last month].
questions.expl: A wish about the past uses had + past participle: hadn't spent.

questions.stem: I wish I had more free time.
questions.expl: Wish plus past simple describes a present situation that is unreal or not as good as desired. Had expresses possession here.

questions.stem: I can't speak French. — ___ can I.
questions.expl: To agree with a negative sentence: Neither can I.

questions.stem: My sister likes K-pop, and so ___ I.
questions.expl: To agree with a positive sentence with likes: so do I.

questions.stem: Not only ___ the report on time, but she also presented it brilliantly.
questions.expl: Not only at the start of a sentence puts the auxiliary first: did she finish.

questions.stem: Rarely ___ such an excellent candidate.
questions.expl: Rarely at the start of a sentence puts the auxiliary first: have we interviewed.

questions.stem: I [was] tired, and [so] [my brother] [was].
questions.fix: was my brother (so was my brother)
questions.expl: So + auxiliary + subject: so was my brother.

questions.stem: [Never] [I have] [heard] [such] a funny story.
questions.expl: Never at the start of a sentence puts the auxiliary first: Never have I heard.

questions.stem: She doesn't eat meat, and neither do I.
questions.expl: Neither do I agrees with a negative statement. Do is the auxiliary for the present simple, and the subject comes after it.

questions.stem: The streets are wet. It ___ rained last night.
questions.expl: A confident guess about the past: must have.

questions.stem: I failed the test. I ___ studied harder.
questions.expl: A regret about the past: should have.

questions.stem: She ___ seen you. She was in Tokyo all week.
questions.expl: Sure that it did not happen: can't have.

questions.stem: I'm not sure where my phone is. I ___ left it in the taxi.
questions.expl: A guess you are not sure about: might have.

questions.stem: You [should] [have] [came] [earlier].
questions.expl: Should have + past participle: come.

questions.stem: He [must] [has] [taken] [the wrong bus].
questions.expl: After must, use the base form have, never has.

questions.stem: You should have brought an umbrella.
questions.expl: Should have plus the past participle brought refers to an expected action that did not happen, often expressing regret or criticism.

questions.stem: The flight was delayed. ___, we missed our connection.
questions.expl: Missing the connection is a result of the delay: As a result.

questions.stem: The software is easy to use. ___, it is very affordable.
questions.expl: We are adding another positive point: Moreover.

questions.stem: Please save your work often. ___, you may lose your data.
questions.expl: Otherwise means 'if you don't do this'.

questions.stem: The product is popular in Asia. ___, sales in Europe remain low.
questions.expl: Popular in Asia but low sales in Europe is a contrast: However.

questions.stem: Many companies now allow remote work. ___, our firm lets staff work from home twice a week.
questions.expl: Our firm is one example of many companies: For example.

questions.stem: Our costs have risen sharply. ___, we must increase our prices.
questions.expl: Raising prices is a result of rising costs: Therefore.

questions.stem: The room [was] small. [Therefore], it was [very] [comfortable].
questions.expl: Small and comfortable is a contrast, not a result: However.

questions.stem: The food was cheap. However, it was delicious.
questions.expl: However connects two contrasting independent sentences. Put a full stop before it and a comma after it.

questions.stem: We offer a ___ guarantee on all products.
questions.expl: A compound adjective with a number stays singular: two-year.

questions.stem: The hotel has a ___ restaurant on the top floor.
questions.expl: A compound adjective with a number is singular and hyphenated: five-star.

questions.stem: Please contact our ___ department for help.
questions.expl: Customer service is a compound noun.

questions.stem: The ___ trained staff handled the problem quickly.
questions.expl: The word describes the adjective trained, so we need an adverb: highly.

questions.stem: We took [a] [fifteen-minutes] [coffee] [break].
questions.expl: A compound adjective with a number stays singular: fifteen-minute.

questions.stem: Our highly experienced team will help you.
questions.expl: Highly is an adverb modifying the adjective experienced. The adverb comes before the adjective in this phrase.

questions.stem: The manager suggested that Mr. Tan ___ the report by Friday.
questions.expl: Suggest that + subject + base verb: submit.

questions.stem: It is essential that all passengers ___ their seatbelts.
questions.expl: It is essential that + base verb: fasten.

questions.stem: The landlord requires that the rent ___ paid on time.
questions.expl: Require that + be + past participle: be paid.

questions.stem: We recommend that she ___ a lawyer before signing.
questions.expl: Recommend that + base verb: consult.

questions.stem: The doctor [recommended] that [she] [drinks] more [water].
questions.expl: Recommend that + base verb, even with she: drink.

questions.stem: I suggest that he apply for the scholarship.
questions.expl: Suggest that can take the base form in a formal recommendation: he apply, not he applies or he to apply.

questions.stem: It was the manager ___ approved the budget.
questions.expl: To emphasise a person, use It was … who (or that).

questions.stem: ___ I need right now is a cup of coffee.
questions.expl: What-cleft: What I need is…

questions.stem: It was in 2010 ___ they opened their first shop.
questions.expl: To emphasise a time: It was + time + that.

questions.stem: [What] I [want] [it] [is] a quiet weekend.
questions.expl: What I want is… Do not add it.

questions.stem: It was my teacher who encouraged me to read more.
questions.expl: This is a cleft sentence. It was my teacher who identifies the person responsible for encouraging me.

questions.stem: ___ you need further information, please call our office.
questions.expl: Should you need… = If you need… (formal).

questions.stem: No sooner had we sat down ___ the phone rang.
questions.expl: No sooner … than.

questions.stem: Hardly had the show started ___ the power went out.
questions.expl: Hardly … when.

questions.stem: Under no circumstances ___ leave the door unlocked.
questions.expl: Under no circumstances is already negative, and it puts the auxiliary first: should you.

questions.stem: Only after checking all the figures ___ the report.
questions.expl: Only after + phrase, then invert the main clause: did she send.

questions.stem: No sooner [I had] [finished] my meal [than] the bill [arrived].
questions.expl: After No sooner, put had before the subject: had I.

questions.stem: Should you need any help, please ask our staff.
questions.expl: Should you need is an inverted formal conditional meaning if you need. In this pattern, should comes before the subject.

questions.stem: Is the shop open on Sunday? — I think ___.
questions.expl: After think, so replaces the whole clause: I think so.

questions.stem: Will we have to work this weekend? — I hope ___.
questions.expl: The negative with hope is I hope not.

questions.stem: These shoes are too small. Do you have bigger ___?
questions.expl: Ones replaces a plural countable noun (shoes).

questions.stem: Tom can play the piano, but his sister ___.
questions.expl: The auxiliary can't stands for can't play the piano.

questions.stem: Do you think she'll come? — I [think] [yes], [but] [I'm] not sure.
questions.expl: After think, use so, not yes: I think so.

questions.stem: I wanted to call you, but I forgot to.
questions.expl: Wanted to call uses the infinitive after wanted. Forgot to avoids repeating call you, so the final to stands for to call you.

questions.stem: Young people ___ to spend more time online.
questions.expl: Young people is plural: tend to + verb.

questions.stem: The project is ___ to be finished by June.
questions.expl: Be likely to + verb means 'will probably'.

questions.stem: I was ___ if you could send me the file.
questions.expl: I was wondering if… is a polite way to ask.

questions.stem: The new policy ___ to have improved staff morale.
questions.expl: The policy is singular: appears to have + past participle.

questions.stem: Sales [are] [likely] [increase] [next] quarter.
questions.expl: Be likely + to + verb: to increase.

questions.stem: It seems that the meeting has been canceled.
questions.expl: Has been canceled is present perfect passive: the meeting received the action, and the result is relevant now.

questions.stem: We would like to ___ you that your order has been shipped.
questions.expl: Formal style: inform somebody that…

questions.stem: Please do not ___ to contact me if you have any questions.
questions.expl: Do not hesitate to contact me is a fixed formal phrase.

questions.stem: I am writing to ___ for the position of sales assistant.
questions.expl: Apply for a position.

questions.stem: Which phrase is the most formal way to end a business email?
questions.expl: Sincerely and Best regards are formal endings.

questions.stem: [Dear] Mr. Brown, I [wanna] [ask] about [the meeting].
questions.expl: A formal email does not use wanna. Use would like to.

questions.stem: We look forward to hearing from you.
questions.expl: Look forward to is a fixed expression. Here to is a preposition, so it is followed by the gerund hearing.

questions.stem: Ms. Rivera was praised for her ___ handling of the client's complaint.
questions.expl: Before the noun handling, we need an adjective: professional.

questions.stem: The new software allows employees to work more ___.
questions.expl: The word describes the verb work, so we need an adverb: efficiently.

questions.stem: All visitors must show proper ___ at the front desk.
questions.expl: After the adjective proper, we need a noun: identification.

questions.stem: The marketing team has ___ improved the company's online presence.
questions.expl: Between has and the past participle, we need an adverb: significantly.

questions.stem: Our hotel is ___ located near the airport and the city center.
questions.expl: The word describes the participle located, so we need an adverb: conveniently.

questions.stem: The director expressed her ___ to all the volunteers.
questions.expl: After her, we need a noun: appreciation.

questions.stem: Please read the safety instructions ___ before using the machine.
questions.expl: The word describes the verb read, so we need an adverb: carefully.

questions.stem: The training session was so ___ that many staff asked for another one.
questions.expl: So + adjective + that: informative.

questions.stem: Mr. Ito is ___ for checking all invoices before payment.
questions.expl: Be responsible for means 'have the job of'.

questions.stem: The company's ___ to quality has earned it many loyal customers.
questions.expl: After company's, we need a noun: commitment.

questions.stem: Applicants should have ___ communication skills.
questions.expl: Before the noun communication skills, we need an adjective: excellent.

questions.stem: The sales figures were ___ higher than last year.
questions.expl: The word describes the comparative higher, so we need an adverb: considerably.

questions.stem: We are ___ to announce the opening of our new branch.
questions.expl: Be pleased to + verb means 'be happy to'.

questions.stem: The museum offers free ___ on the first Sunday of every month.
questions.expl: After the adjective free, we need a noun: admission.

questions.stem: Our technicians will respond ___ to any service request.
questions.expl: The word describes the verb respond, so we need an adverb: promptly.

questions.stem: The proposal was rejected because it was not financially ___.
questions.expl: After be and the adverb financially, we need an adjective: feasible.

questions.stem: Ms. Garcia is one of the most ___ designers in the company.
questions.expl: The most + adjective + noun: creative.

questions.stem: The ___ of the new factory will create 500 jobs.
questions.expl: The … of needs a noun: construction.

questions.stem: Employees must complete the form ___ and return it to HR.
questions.expl: The word describes the verb complete, so we need an adverb: accurately.

questions.stem: The CEO gave a very ___ speech at the annual dinner.
questions.expl: The speech gave people inspiration, so we use the -ing adjective: inspiring.

questions.stem: We were ___ by the high quality of the samples.
questions.expl: We describes people's feelings, so we use the -ed adjective: impressed.

questions.stem: The new parking rules will become ___ on July 1.
questions.expl: Become effective means 'start to apply'.

questions.stem: The board of directors ___ the merger at next week's meeting.
questions.expl: Next week is in the future: will discuss.

questions.stem: Since joining the company, Mr. Ahmed ___ three major projects.
questions.expl: Since + a starting point shows a period up to now: has managed.

questions.stem: The package ___ to the wrong address yesterday.
questions.expl: Yesterday + passive: was sent.

questions.stem: Currently, our engineers ___ a new mobile application.
questions.expl: Currently signals the present continuous.

questions.stem: The conference room ___ for the training session tomorrow.
questions.expl: The room receives the action, and the booking is already done: has been reserved.

questions.stem: By the end of this year, the company ___ 20 new stores.
questions.expl: By the end of + a future time: future perfect, will have opened.

questions.stem: Last quarter, profits ___ by nearly 10 percent.
questions.expl: Last quarter is a finished past time: rise → rose.

questions.stem: Ms. Lopez usually ___ the weekly sales report on Fridays.
questions.expl: Usually + a singular subject: prepares.

questions.stem: All orders ___ within two business days.
questions.expl: Orders receive the action: are processed.

questions.stem: When the fire alarm rang, the employees ___ a meeting.
questions.expl: An action in progress that was interrupted uses the past continuous.

questions.stem: The new policy ___ by the board last Monday.
questions.expl: The policy receives the action, last Monday: was approved.

questions.stem: Please make sure that the lights ___ off before you leave.
questions.expl: The lights receive the action: are turned off.

questions.stem: Mr. Park ___ for the company for over twenty years when he retired.
questions.expl: Before a past moment (when he retired): past perfect.

questions.stem: If sales ___ to grow, we will hire more staff.
questions.expl: First conditional: If + present simple.

questions.stem: The quarterly meeting will be held ___ the third floor.
questions.expl: Floors take on: on the third floor.

questions.stem: Payment is due ___ receipt of the invoice.
questions.expl: Upon receipt means 'as soon as it is received'.

questions.stem: The store will be closed ___ the holiday period.
questions.expl: Throughout + a period means 'for the whole of it'.

questions.stem: Ms. Lee has worked in sales ___ 2015.
questions.expl: A starting point in time: since.

questions.stem: The report must be submitted ___ Friday at 5 p.m.
questions.expl: By means 'not later than' for a deadline.

questions.stem: The bus stop is located directly ___ the hotel entrance.
questions.expl: Opposite means 'facing, on the other side'.

questions.stem: The museum is open daily ___ 9 a.m. to 6 p.m.
questions.expl: From … to … shows a time range.

questions.stem: Refunds will be issued ___ 14 days of the return.
questions.expl: Within + a period means 'inside that time'.

questions.stem: The training is mandatory for all staff, ___ managers.
questions.expl: Including works as a preposition: it adds part of a group.

questions.stem: The meeting was postponed ___ the director's illness.
questions.expl: The director's illness is a noun phrase: because of.

questions.stem: The lecture was interesting, ___ a bit too long.
questions.expl: Albeit means 'although' and is followed by an adjective or phrase. It is formal.

questions.stem: Customers can pay ___ cash or by credit card.
questions.expl: Pay in cash, but pay by card.

questions.stem: Ms. Clark is responsible ___ training new employees.
questions.expl: Responsible for + noun or -ing.

questions.stem: The price of the tour includes meals and accommodation, but not ___ insurance.
questions.expl: Travel insurance is a compound noun.

questions.stem: We apologize ___ any inconvenience this may cause.
questions.expl: Apologise for something.

questions.stem: Please reply ___ this email by Thursday.
questions.expl: Reply to something.

questions.stem: ___ the weather was bad, the outdoor concert went ahead as planned.
questions.expl: A clause with a contrasting meaning: Although.

questions.stem: You will not be able to enter the building ___ you show your ID card.
questions.expl: Unless means 'if not'.

questions.stem: Ms. Brown will lead the meeting ___ Mr. Davis is on vacation.
questions.expl: Mr. Davis is on vacation is a clause: while.

questions.stem: Both the manager ___ her assistant attended the conference.
questions.expl: Both … and.

questions.stem: Please arrive early ___ we can start the meeting on time.
questions.expl: So that shows purpose.

questions.stem: Neither the printer ___ the scanner is working today.
questions.expl: Neither … nor.

questions.stem: The shop offers free delivery ___ the order is over $50.
questions.expl: A condition: if.

questions.stem: ___ submitting the form, check that all information is correct.
questions.expl: Before + -ing.

questions.stem: The first design was simple, ___ the second one was more detailed.
questions.expl: Whereas contrasts two clauses.

questions.stem: ___ you have any questions, please contact our support team.
questions.expl: A condition: If.

questions.stem: The project was completed on time ___ several unexpected problems.
questions.expl: Several unexpected problems is a noun phrase: in spite of.

questions.stem: Not only did the hotel upgrade our room, ___ it also gave us free breakfast.
questions.expl: Not only … but also.

questions.stem: We will not start the meeting ___ everyone has arrived.
questions.expl: Not … until means 'only when'.

questions.stem: ___ the hotel nor the restaurant accepts credit cards.
questions.expl: Neither … nor.

questions.stem: Ms. Kim asked that all reports be sent directly to ___.
questions.expl: After the preposition to, we need an object pronoun: her.

questions.stem: The employees organized the farewell party by ___.
questions.expl: By themselves means 'without help'.

questions.stem: Mr. Chen forgot ___ laptop in the meeting room.
questions.expl: Before the noun laptop, we need a possessive adjective: his.

questions.stem: Our products are cheaper than ___ of our competitors.
questions.expl: Those replaces a plural noun already mentioned (products).

questions.stem: ___ who wish to join the tour should sign up at the front desk.
questions.expl: Those who means 'the people who'.

questions.stem: The company celebrated ___ 50th anniversary last month.
questions.expl: The company is singular, so the possessive is its. It's means it is.

questions.stem: The guests said they enjoyed ___ stay at our hotel.
questions.expl: Before the noun stay, we need a possessive adjective: their.

questions.stem: Mr. Diaz prefers to review the contracts ___ before signing them.
questions.expl: Himself emphasises that he does it personally.

questions.stem: Please ___ the attached file for the meeting agenda.
questions.expl: Refer to means 'look at for information'.

questions.stem: The hotel offers a free airport ___ service for all guests.
questions.expl: An airport shuttle is a bus or car that takes guests to and from the airport.

questions.stem: Due to high ___, the new phone sold out in two days.
questions.expl: High demand means many people want to buy it.

questions.stem: All employees must ___ the new safety regulations.
questions.expl: Comply with rules means 'obey them'.

questions.stem: The company will ___ all travel expenses for the conference.
questions.expl: Reimburse expenses means 'pay back money someone has spent'.

questions.stem: The job ___ was posted on the company website last week.
questions.expl: A job opening is a position that needs to be filled.

questions.stem: We need to ___ the deadline because the materials arrived late.
questions.expl: Extend a deadline means 'give more time'.

questions.stem: The warranty ___ all repairs for two years.
questions.expl: A warranty covers repairs: it includes them.

questions.stem: Ms. Ortiz was ___ to regional manager after five years.
questions.expl: Be promoted to means 'be given a higher position'.

questions.stem: Our customer service team is ___ 24 hours a day.
questions.expl: Available means 'ready to help or be used'.

questions.stem: Please ___ a table for six at 7 p.m.
questions.expl: Reserve a table means 'book it in advance'.

questions.stem: The flight was ___ because of heavy fog.
questions.expl: A delayed flight leaves later than planned.

questions.stem: The manager asked us to ___ our ideas at the next meeting.
questions.expl: Ask somebody to + base verb: present.

questions.stem: To ___ for the discount, customers must spend at least $50.
questions.expl: Qualify for means 'meet the conditions to get'.

questions.stem: The new manager quickly ___ a good relationship with her team.
questions.expl: Establish a relationship means 'build it'.

questions.stem: Interested candidates should ___ their résumés by email.
questions.expl: Submit a résumé means 'send it officially'.

questions.stem: The factory is running at full ___ to meet the holiday orders.
questions.expl: At full capacity means 'producing as much as possible'.

questions.stem: We will ___ you as soon as your order is ready.
questions.expl: Notify somebody means 'tell them officially'.

questions.stem: Please keep your receipt as ___ of purchase.
questions.expl: Proof of purchase shows that you bought something.

questions.stem: The company plans to ___ its business into three new markets.
questions.expl: Expand into new markets means 'grow into them'.

questions.stem: Staff are ___ to wear their ID badges at all times.
questions.expl: Be required to means 'must'.

questions.stem: The concert was canceled, and all ticket holders will receive a full ___.
questions.expl: A refund is money paid back.

questions.stem: Our sales ___ have increased by 20 percent.
questions.expl: Sales figures are the numbers that show sales.

questions.stem: The hotel was fully ___, so we had to stay somewhere else.
questions.expl: Fully booked means there are no free rooms.

questions.stem: The two companies have agreed to ___ on the new project.
questions.expl: Collaborate on means 'work together on'.

questions.stem: The CEO will ___ the opening speech at the conference.
questions.expl: Deliver a speech means 'give a speech'.

questions.stem: Please ___ from smoking inside the building.
questions.expl: Refrain from + -ing means 'do not do'. It is formal.

questions.stem: The bank will ___ a fee for international transfers.
questions.expl: Charge a fee means 'ask for money for a service'.

questions.stem: This year's conference attracted ___ participants than last year's.
questions.expl: Comparative + than: more participants.

questions.stem: This is the ___ sales result in the company's history.
questions.expl: The + superlative: the best.

questions.stem: The new model is ___ lighter than the old one.
questions.expl: Much makes a comparative stronger: much lighter. Very cannot go before a comparative.

questions.stem: ___ employee will receive a bonus this year.
questions.expl: Every + singular noun: every employee.

questions.stem: There were ___ complaints about the new menu.
questions.expl: Complaints is countable, so we use few.

questions.stem: The candidate ___ we interviewed yesterday has accepted the offer.
questions.expl: The person is the object of interviewed: whom (or who, that).

questions.stem: The building ___ the conference will be held has a large parking lot.
questions.expl: For a place (= in which): where.

questions.stem: Thank you for ___ our survey.
questions.expl: After a preposition (for), use -ing.

questions.stem: We look forward to ___ with you again.
questions.expl: Look forward to + -ing.

questions.stem: The manager decided ___ the event until next month.
questions.expl: Decide + to + verb.

questions.stem: Customers who wish ___ their orders should call before noon.
questions.expl: Wish + to + verb.

questions.stem: ___ the end of the year, all employees will receive a gift card.
questions.expl: At the end of a period.

questions.stem: The marketing manager, ___ ideas helped increase sales, will speak first.
questions.expl: Whose shows possession: the manager's ideas.

questions.stem: Please inform us ___ any changes to your address.
questions.expl: Inform somebody of something.

questions.stem: The software update is ___ to fix the login problem.
questions.expl: Be expected to means 'should happen, according to plans'.

questions.stem: The accounting department will ___ the revised budget by Friday afternoon.
questions.expl: After will, use the base-form verb circulate. The department will send the budget to the relevant staff.

questions.stem: Employees are asked to keep their identification cards ___ at all times.
questions.expl: Keep is followed by an object complement. Visible describes the cards' state, while the other choices are nouns or an adverb.

questions.stem: The supplier promised to deliver the replacement parts ___ than expected.
questions.expl: The word than calls for the comparative adverb sooner. The sentence compares the promised delivery time with the expected time.

questions.stem: The customer service team has received several ___ about the delayed shipment.
questions.expl: Several must modify a plural countable noun. Complaints fits the meaning and the grammar; the other forms are verb forms.

questions.stem: Please submit the travel request ___ you book the hotel.
questions.expl: Before introduces the earlier action. Employees should submit the request first and book the hotel afterward.

questions.stem: The new printer is capable ___ producing color brochures.
questions.expl: Capable is followed by the preposition of and a gerund. Producing completes the phrase capable of producing.

questions.stem: Ms. Patel will attend the conference ___ her supervisor is unavailable.
